name: PT Darma Henwa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Darma Henwa: a real fleet turnaround, a rate-led revenue line and a copper option priced on faith
frontmatter.summary: Darma Henwa's owned fleet has lifted margins and cash generation, but revenue growth is rate-led while client volumes fall and capex has not stepped down. The shares now trade at a premium to our fundamental value after the GMR appraisal is probability-weighted; we rate the stock HOLD with a Rp271 target that holds part of the konglo premium.
thesis: The in-house fleet is real. The owned batches lifted the gross margin to 20.2% in our forecast and the subcontractor line fell to IDR593.4bn in the first nine months of 2026; this is operating leverage from a completed capital programme, not a coal-price windfall [S4, S6].

Revenue is rate-led, not volume-led. KPC's own mine output fell in FY2025 and the nine-month revenue increase came from higher rates and the Arutmin extension, so we forecast growth of 8.5% then 5.0%, not a volume cycle [S3, S4].

Capex has not stepped down. Nine-month capex was flat year on year at IDR1,341.6bn and a subsidiary drew new equipment credit in October 2026; we hold FY2026E capex at 25.0% of revenue and the long-run rate above D&A [S4, S10, F52, F105].

GMR is the swing factor, and we now weight it. The copper-gold asset is carried at its IDR844.5bn consideration floor plus half of the KJPP appraisal uplift, because there is still no resource, reserve or feasibility statement; a full write-back to consideration would remove a further IDR4,535.4bn of value [S4, S5, F19, F20].

The konglo lens does the regime work. Price is 1.45x our current fundamental value of Rp181; with no HSC listing, no enforcement and a compliant free float [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026], the base regime keeps part of the log premium over twelve months, leaving the target above our twelve-month value [S0].

We rate DEWA HOLD with a Rp271 target, 4.5% total return. The price already exceeds our twelve-month fundamental value; the target is a konglo-lens premium, not a fundamental discount, and the rating is sensitive to the GMR bridge [S0].

blocks.text: **What changed and why.** This revision answers the red team on the two judgements that carried the previous ADD: the GMR bridge and the contract-life terminal. GMR is no longer carried at the full KJPP appraisal. We keep the IDR844.5bn consideration as a full floor, as the method card requires, and weight the IDR4,535.4bn appraisal uplift at half — the midpoint of the only two observed values — because there is still no public resource, reserve or feasibility statement to adjudicate [S5, F19, F20]. We also cut terminal growth to 3.0% to reflect the falling delivered volumes and the absence of a contracted renewal, rebased the borrowing line to the 30 September 2026 gross debt, and corrected the FY2026 P&L for the nine-month other income already booked [S4, S5, F71, F73]. The weighted fundamental value is Rp179; the share price is Rp262, a premium of 1.45x that value. The konglo lens keeps part of that premium over twelve months and produces a Rp271 target, a 4.5% total return including the Rp3 dividend [S0]. The rating moves from ADD to HOLD; the operating facts are unchanged.

DEWA is a coal-mining services contractor that spent the last two years converting itself from a subcontracted labour broker into an owner of heavy equipment. The operating evidence is in the numbers: nine-month revenue of IDR5,102.0bn came against IDR4,650.4bn a year earlier, gross profit reached IDR1,034.8bn, and the subcontractor line in cost of revenues fell to IDR593.4bn as the owned fleet took over waste removal [S4]. The company is no longer a pure pass-through of someone else's mining plan.

The growth, however, is not a volume cycle. KPC's revenue rose while its own mine output fell: overburden removal at the KPC project was 102 million bcm in FY2025 against 106 million bcm in FY2024 and coal production was 10.5 million tonnes against 11.2 million tonnes [S3, F71, F72, F74, F75]. The nine-month increase came from rates, mix and the Arutmin extension, not from more material moved, and the company does not publish quarterly physical volumes [S4]. That distinction matters for the forecast: a contractor paid per cubic metre cannot compound a rate increase the way a miner compounds a commodity price.

The market has moved the other way. DEWA shares trade at Rp262, well below their twelve-month high of Rp815, after the Indonesian concentrated-ownership complex de-rated through 2026 [S0, S9]. Our current fundamental value is Rp181 and our twelve-month value is Rp207; the price is 1.45x the current value, so the market is no longer paying less than the contract business plus GMR is worth today. We do not treat that as a reason to bend the fundamentals: the model values the contract business on its own cash flows to the end of the client licences and carries the GMR copper-gold asset at its consideration plus half the appraisal uplift, then lets the konglo lens decide how much of the small premium closes. That lens produces a Rp271 target and our HOLD rating.

The variant view is narrow and uncomfortable. The contract business alone is worth materially less than the share price, and the rest of the equity value is GMR, an asset for which the market does not pay the independent appraisal [S5]. Market capitalisation is IDR10,230.7bn and the GMR bridge is the IDR844.5bn consideration plus half of the IDR4,535.4bn appraisal uplift, so the asset accounts for more than half of the equity value while the contract business trades below our DCF [S0, S5, F18, F20]. The market is not marking GMR at zero, but it is not paying the full appraisal either. If GMR is real, the stock is cheap; if it is not, the downside is the contract business and the debt that funds it. We weight the appraisal at half rather than taking it whole, because the method card forbids a default haircut below sourced sunk value but the asset has no resource, reserve or feasibility statement to support the full KJPP number; the full write-back to consideration is the tail in the risk section [S5, F18, F20].

What moves the value: first, GMR exploration and permitting news, because it is the largest single asset in the valuation; second, the durability of the KPC and Arutmin contracts through the RKAB cut and the state-exporter transition; third, capex, which has not yet stepped down and is the reason free cash flow is thinner than the fleet story implies [S3, S4, S7]. The two things that could break the thesis are a GMR write-down and a related-party contract reset on worse terms. The rating is a HOLD: 4.5% total return is below the house ADD threshold, so the shares are neither cheap enough to buy nor expensive enough to sell, and the target is above our twelve-month value only because the konglo lens keeps part of the small premium the shares already carry.

PT Darma Henwa Tbk is a general mining contractor listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 2007, providing integrated mining services from land clearing and overburden removal through coal getting, hauling and port handling [S3, S6]. It reports two segments, mining services and other services, and the business is overwhelmingly the first: overburden removal and coal production for two coal-mining clients in Kalimantan. The company employed 5,184 people at the last count [S0].

The revenue model is rate-based, not commodity-based. DEWA is paid for material moved and coal produced and hauled, so its top line follows its clients' mine plans and the rates negotiated in the operating agreements. In FY2025 the company moved 139 million bcm of overburden and produced 17.0 million tonnes of coal [S3, F21, F22]. The trend under those totals is the important part: KPC's waste removal fell to 102 million bcm from 106 million bcm in FY2024 and 122 million bcm in FY2023, while Arutmin's rose to 36.5 million bcm from a depressed 28.0 million bcm but remained below its 54.0 million bcm level two years earlier [S3, F71, F72, F73, F77, F78, F79]. Coal output followed the same path, with KPC at 10.5 million tonnes against 11.2 million tonnes and Arutmin at 6.5 million tonnes against 6.1 million tonnes [S3, F74, F75, F80, F81]. This is a contractor whose clients were already moving less material before the national quota cut.

The fleet split is the strategic story. 95.2 million bcm of waste removal and 12.5 million tonnes of coal came from the in-house fleet in FY2025, leaving subcontractors to move 46.9 million bcm of overburden; the two batches added 30.0 million bcm p.a. and 25.0 million bcm p.a. of annual capacity and were fully operational by the end of September 2025 [S3, S6, F25, F26, F36, F37, F83].

The client base is the defining feature of the business. In FY2025, 95.5% of revenue came from related-party customers, principally PT Kaltim Prima Coal and PT Arutmin Indonesia, both described in the financial statements as entities under common control with DEWA [S3, S5]. In the first nine months of 2026, KPC supplied IDR3,588.0bn of revenue and Arutmin IDR1,395.0bn, with third parties only IDR119.0bn; the related-party share rose to 97.7% of revenue as third-party work fell [S4, F31, F32, F33, F87]. KPC's work is the Bengalon coal-mining project in East Kalimantan plus the Lubuk Tutung coal-port operation, run through the Dire Pratama subsidiary; Arutmin's work is the Asam Asam project and its Kintap East and Kintap West extensions in South Kalimantan [S3].

The contract terms are the asset life. KPC's agreements were signed on 1 May 2023 for the life of the mine, with its IUPK valid to 31 December 2031; Arutmin's agreements were extended on 19 January 2026, also for the life of the mine, with its IUPK valid to 1 November 2030 [S5, F91, F92]. Those two dates, not a perpetuity, are the explicit life of the contract business; the DCF stops in FY2031 and treats anything beyond as renewal value.

The strategy has three legs: fleet ownership and vertical integration, now largely complete; cost discipline; and diversification beyond coal through GMR, a copper-gold exploration project at Gayo Lues in Aceh in which DEWA acquired an indirect 99.8% stake in 2025 [S3, S5]. Management calls the next phase a "light asset model" — a claim the October equipment credit sits awkwardly beside [S3, S10].

DEWA is a challenger, not the leader, in Indonesian mining services: the large contract miners operate bigger fleets and broader client books, while DEWA is a specialist supplier to one corporate group. That is both the source of its contract visibility and the source of its governance discount. The company is identified as a Bakrie-group name by the Indonesian press, and its two main customers are entities under common control with it, which is how the house konglo registry classifies it [S8, S9; house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026].

Indonesian mining contractors sit between the coal miners and the equipment makers. They are paid per cubic metre moved or tonne hauled, carry the diesel, maintenance and labour risk, and are only as busy as their clients' mine plans; contractors with owned equipment tend to earn steadier margins than subcontracted operators.

The addressable market is Indonesian coal-mine services, sized by how much overburden the miners must strip and how much coal they are permitted to produce. The policy lever is the annual RKAB quota, which the annual report records was cut from 790 million tonnes in 2025 to 600 million tonnes in 2026 [S3, F38, F39]. A smaller national quota does not mechanically cut contractor volumes — the mix shifts toward whichever mines keep their allocations — but it caps the services pool and strengthens the bargaining power of the miners that allocate work. DEWA's own projects show the pool was already shrinking at the margin, with KPC's waste removal down over two years and Arutmin's recovery only partial [S3, F71, F72, F73, F77, F78, F79].

The second policy lever is the export channel. From 1 January 2027, coal exports must be handled by the state vehicle PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia; existing registered-exporter permits run only to the end of 2026, and the industry association has warned that the handover could disrupt cargoes [S7]. For a contractor the direct exposure is second-order — DEWA is paid by the miner, not the export buyer — but a disruption to client shipments feeds quickly into mine plans, payment timing and receivables.

The commodity backdrop is neutral rather than hostile: the house coal deck carries Newcastle at US$118/t and the HBA at US$112/t for FY2027E, above the long-run marker, while spot Newcastle is US$150/t (house coal deck, reviewed). Contractor rates do not rise with coal prices; the rate is negotiated and the client keeps the commodity upside. The cost side matters more: the house Brent deck runs at US$96.0/bbl for FY2026E, easing to US$84.0/bbl for FY2027E against a spot of US$95.7/bbl (house Brent deck, reviewed). We pass only half of the oil move into rates in the same year, so a higher Brent path compresses the margin rather than breaking the model [S4]. The new equipment credit carries a marginal rate of 10.0% per annum, so the cost of fleet renewal has risen, not fallen [S10, F106].

Competitive positioning is best described through the five forces, because no reliable public share data exists for Indonesian mining services. Buyer power is very high: two related-party clients dominate revenue and set rates and payment terms [S5, S8]. Supplier power is moderate, new entry is moderate at the small end and low at the large-project end, and substitutes are limited to in-sourcing or rival contractors. Rivalry is intense, but the related-party relationship blunts it for the KPC and Arutmin work. The moat is therefore contractual and operational rather than geological: DEWA owns operating agreements with two mines under common control and a fleet that lowers its unit cost. The relevant "reserve life" is the contract life, which is why the explicit DCF stops at FY2031 and the terminal value is disclosed as renewal [S5, F91, F92].

The macro tilt the frame carries is mixed. The house macro regime is balance-of-payments pressure with a cautious stance; thermal coal is neutral and Indonesian rate-sensitive names are on the avoid list (house macro deck, reviewed). DEWA is domestic, rupiah-earning and leveraged, so the rate-sensitive tilt is a headwind; expensive oil is a cost headwind through diesel. Neither tilt overrides the company-specific contract and asset facts [S3, S4].

Mining services is a cyclical, capital-heavy business with few structural moats. Contractors win work on safety record, fleet availability and price, and lose it when a client changes mine plan or brings work in-house. The best operators run first-quartile unit costs and keep utilisation high through the cycle; the weakest carry idle equipment and subcontract the overflow. Indonesia adds a policy layer because production quotas, export rules and royalty regimes change with each administration.

The financial history is a turnaround with one enormous accounting distortion. Revenue was IDR6,068.5bn in FY2022, IDR7,372.7bn in FY2023, IDR6,032.0bn in FY2024 and IDR6,392.8bn in FY2025, so the top line has grown only modestly while the cost base changed completely [S5]. The reported net profit of IDR4,306.7bn in FY2025 is not an operating number: it contains a non-cash negative goodwill gain of IDR4,535.4bn from the GMR acquisition, which is why the reported margin and return on equity look absurd [S5, F18]. Stripping out the non-cash other-net items, the underlying business earned a modest profit; the nine-month 2026 result of IDR513.1bn is the cleaner read on current earning power [S4, S8].

The revenue build starts from the nine-month run-rate and is deliberately decomposed by client, because that is the only decomposition the filing supports. Nine-month revenue of IDR5,102.0bn compared with IDR4,650.4bn a year earlier, but KPC supplied IDR3,588.0bn against IDR3,088.0bn and Arutmin IDR1,395.0bn against IDR1,357.9bn, while third-party revenue fell to IDR119.0bn from IDR204.4bn [S4, F28, F31, F32, F33, F70, F84, F85, F86]. KPC's revenue therefore grew despite lower own-mine output, which means the increase is a rate and scope effect, not a volume effect; the company does not disclose quarterly bcm or tonnes, so the precise split cannot be observed [S3, S4]. We carry the run-rate into FY2026E growth of 8.5%, below the nine-month pace, and then 5.0%, 4.0%, 3.5% and 3.0% as flat-to-down client volumes meet the lower national RKAB and the state-exporter transition [S3, S4, S7]. No public mine-plan volume schedule exists for FY2027E-FY2030E; we do not invent one, and we hold volumes flat with rate inflation.

The margin story is the core of the case. FY2025 gross margin was 15.1%; the first nine months of 2026 ran at IDR1,034.8bn of gross profit on IDR5,102.0bn of revenue, a realised margin of well over a fifth [S4, F28, F59]. The reason is visible in the cost lines: subcontractor cost fell to IDR593.4bn, while repair and maintenance was IDR758.3bn, salaries IDR661.0bn and fuel only IDR210.8bn [S4]. Owning the fleet converts a variable subcontractor cost into fixed depreciation and maintenance, so incremental volume drops through at a high margin. We model an effective FY2026E gross margin of 20.2% and hold the input flat in nominal terms thereafter: costs stay at the last actual in real terms, and the effective margin moves only with the oil link [S3, S4]. G&A is held at the observed nine-month run-rate because the interim LK gives no basis to treat the salary step as non-recurring [S4].

Depreciation is the line the data pack gets most wrong, and our restatement is deliberately conservative. IDX filings use the direct cash-flow method, so the vendor data carries a D&A charge that is a fraction of the real one; the financial statements show total FY2025 depreciation and amortisation of IDR940.7bn, of which right-of-use depreciation was IDR78.7bn [S5, F9, F10]. The company's own EBITDA bridge is IDR1,752.6bn, against operating profit of IDR726.4bn, implying a total non-cash charge above the two printed depreciation lines [S3, F88, F89]. For the first nine months of 2026 the LK prints fixed-asset depreciation of IDR826.2bn and right-of-use depreciation of IDR19.1bn, together over a sixth of revenue [S4, F110, F111]. Our FY2025A D&A line uses that combined total, giving FY2025A EBITDA of IDR1,667.1bn against the company's IDR1,752.6bn bridge; the residual gap is unprinted amortisation and other non-cash items, which we disclose rather than force into D&A [S3, S4, S5].

Cash flow and capital allocation tell the same transition story, but they do not yet show the harvest. FY2025 free cash flow to the firm was IDR-502.6bn, negative because capex of IDR1,588.9bn absorbed the fleet build and working capital swung [S5]. By the first nine months of 2026 capex was IDR1,341.6bn, flat on the prior-year period and equal to over a quarter of nine-month revenue, while the company also spent IDR791.4bn of cash on treasury shares and paid the FY2025 dividend of IDR58.6bn [S3, S4, F15, F52, F107]. Those outflows were funded with new bank debt: bank loans rose to IDR2,268.9bn current and IDR2,306.0bn non-current at 30 September 2026, from gross debt of IDR3,559.4bn at the prior year-end, while cash fell to IDR744.9bn [S4, F34, F103, F104]. The October equipment credit of IDR149.2bn to a subsidiary, explicitly for heavy‑equipment purchase, shows the capex cycle is not over [S10, F105]. We hold FY2026E capex at 25.0% of revenue and let it ease to a long-run rate above D&A so the fleet is maintained rather than run down [S4, S6, S10].

The balance sheet at the interim date is the one that matters, and it is fully traced in the LK's own cash-flow statement. At 30 September 2026 the company carried current bank loans of IDR2,268.9bn and non-current bank loans of IDR2,306.0bn against cash of IDR744.9bn, and the LK's own net‑debt figure is the one the DCF uses [S4, F34, F103, F104]. Gross debt ties to the model: the model's FY2026E gross debt of IDR4,630.3bn is the bank loans plus lease liabilities at 30 September — a sourced actual, not a forecast — and the net‑borrowing input contains only the change in gross bank debt, not the other financing and investing outflows that moved cash. Those outflows appear in the LK's cash‑flow table: nine‑month operating cash of IDR1,664.8bn, nine‑month investing cash of IDR2,158.2bn, nine‑month financing cash of IDR352.4bn, and within those totals the IDR791.4bn treasury purchase, the net repayment of other long‑term payables and the nine‑month investing that sits outside the capex line (advances for fixed assets, exploration, other non‑current placements and other current assets) [S4 p.12‑13]. The model's single borrowing line cannot encode them; we do not force them through the working‑capital or other‑non‑operating–line inputs because that would corrupt the DCF's own free cash flow. Carrying those lines through the LK's own totals gives a year‑end cash figure close to the 30 September actual, because our fourth quarter is roughly cash‑neutral; the model's FY2026E cash line is higher solely by the financing and investing outflows listed here, so the summary table's net‑debt/EBITDA row should be read on the interim actual rather than on that line. The DCF bridge therefore uses the 30 September actual net debt, not the mechanical roll, and reconciles the gap as a note rather than a modelling failure [S4, F34]. Interest cover is thin: nine-month gross profit of IDR1,034.8bn less G&A of IDR322.4bn against finance cost of IDR319.4bn is only a little over two times, and the forecast interest bill rises with the higher marginal rate we now use [S4, F60, F61, F106]. Working capital is unusual: the FY2025 operating working capital position was negative at IDR-227.6bn, because related-party payables and receivables net close; at the end of September 2026, trade receivables from related parties had risen to IDR1,818.3bn from IDR1,537.2bn at the prior year-end, against nine-month revenue of IDR5,102.0bn [S4, S5, F28, F68, F69]. That is a high balance, but it is the mirror of the related-party model. Operating cash flow of IDR1,664.8bn in the nine months was healthy enough to cover interest and part of capex, but not the buyback [S4, F108]. The forecast assumes no new net borrowing after FY2026E, with capex normalising and free cash flow covering debt service [S4]; that is the most likely path only if the fleet stays utilised and the related-party rates hold.

Earnings-quality flags, following the house screen, are mostly optics-class rather than manipulation-class, but the capital-allocation record is poor. The accruals ratio is meaningless in FY2025 because the negative goodwill is non-cash and enormous; normalised, operating cash flow of IDR1,456.1bn was healthy against underlying profit [S5, F47]. Related-party trade receivables are large and rising, but disclosed and consistent with the client base [S4, F68]. The FY2025 result also carries non-cash write-offs of receivables, inventory and fixed assets, which we exclude from the forecast as one-offs [S5]. The structure flags are real and disclosed: the 2025 debt-to-equity conversion issued new Series B shares at Rp75 to three creditors, and the 2026 buyback authorised up to IDR950.0bn and paid IDR791.4bn of cash for 1,639 million shares at an average far above today's price, with the shares held as treasury rather than retired [S3, F54, F56, F93, F107]. We classify these as optics-class and haircut nothing in the base, but they are the reason the governance section matters.

We value DEWA with a contract-life discounted cash flow as the primary method, because the company's asset is a set of operating agreements with a finite, dated life, not a commodity reserve. The industry card's through-cycle NAV logic translates directly: the "life of asset" is the contract base, anchored on the Arutmin IUPK to 1 November 2030 and the KPC IUPK to 31 December 2031 [S5, F91, F92]. The explicit forecast runs only to FY2031; the terminal value after that is the value of renewal, not contracted volume. One timing point: FY2031E sits inside KPC's licence, but for Arutmin, whose IUPK expires on 1 November 2030, it is a full twelve months of assumed renewal, with FY2030E carrying the November‑December stub after expiry; so the final explicit year already assumes an Arutmin renewal for roughly a quarter of revenue [S5, F92]. The cost side is priced off the house Brent deck through the oil link; there is no revenue commodity price to mark to a benchmark, which is why this is a corporate FCFF model rather than a commodity-producer NAV [S0, S4]. We cross-check with EV/EBITDA and EV/Sales, the two multiples contractors are actually traded on, and drop P/E because the FY2025 earnings base is contaminated by negative goodwill [S5].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro inputs: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 1.00 from the industry default, relevered to 1.35 at the company's debt-to-equity ratio, a one-point size premium and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% [S0, S4]. The WACC keeps the house pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%; the separate P&L interest rate is what drives the forecast interest charge — the nine-month finance charge annualised on average debt is about a tenth, and the new equipment facility carries 10.0% per annum — but it does not change the WACC's cost of debt [S4, S10, F106]. That gives a cost of equity of 15.9% and a WACC of 13.2%, with debt at 31.2% of the capital structure [S0]. The WACC is high because the name is small, leveraged and Indonesian; it is not a discretionary haircut.

The DCF produces a value of Rp168 per share, with the terminal value accounting for 66.9% of enterprise value [S0]. That is a high terminal share and we disclose it: in a contract-life model the terminal value is the value of renewing the KPC and Arutmin agreements after FY2031, not a perpetuity on contracted volume [S5, F91, F92]. A reader who believes neither client renews should strip it out and treat the final year as contingent; what remains is the documented cash flows plus the GMR asset [S0, S5, F92]. Enterprise value is IDR7,311.0bn [S0]. The bridge to equity carries GMR at the IDR844.5bn consideration as a full floor plus half of the IDR4,535.4bn KJPP appraisal uplift, which is the weighted carry the valuation table and the scenario section use. The appraisal values net identifiable assets at IDR6,699.1bn less the deferred tax liability of IDR1,305.8bn, and at 99.8% ownership the uplift over consideration is exactly the negative goodwill of IDR4,535.4bn, so the base takes half of it and withholds half [S5, F19, F20, F46, F90]. The bridge then subtracts net debt at 30 September 2026: cash of IDR744.9bn against bank loans of IDR2,268.9bn current and IDR2,306.0bn non-current, plus lease liabilities [S4, S5, F34, F103, F104]. That choice matters: the 2026 buyback absorbed IDR791.4bn of cash after the year-end balance sheet, and a modelled roll would flatter the equity value [S4, F107].

The GMR carrying value is the largest single judgement in the report, and it is a probability weight rather than a single appraisal number. The asset is an independent appraiser's fair value of net identifiable assets less deferred tax, and the consideration is the sunk value the method card requires us to keep [S5, F19, F20]. There is still no published resource, reserve or feasibility study, and the subsidiary table lists the project as not yet operating [S4, F109]. An asset-value floor is not an NPV, and we say so. We therefore carry the consideration floor in full and the IDR4,535.4bn appraisal uplift at half — the midpoint of the only two observed values — which puts half of the uplift in the base and leaves the other half withheld. If the appraisal is not validated, the asset is written back to the IDR844.5bn consideration and the bridge loses that withheld half, about a third of the fundamental value of Rp179; that is the quantified GMR downside and it sits on top of the mechanical bear case [S5, F18, F20]. We do not add a success premium. For a reader who marks GMR at zero, the whole company costs IDR10,230.7bn of market capitalisation plus net debt against a DCF contract-business enterprise value of IDR7,311.0bn [S0].

The cross-checks bracket the DCF, the honest outcome for a contractor with a large non-operating asset [S0]. EV/EBITDA at the peer median of 7.1x gives Rp283; EV/Sales at 0.9x gives Rp125. The weights are 70% DCF, 15% EV/EBITDA and 15% EV/Sales, so the multiples carry under a third of the value [S0]. The EBITDA leg is the least reliable: its peer median sits on a mining-services-and-coal peer set while PTRO trades far above it on a konglo premium, and the metric is the engine's IDR1,667.1bn, below the company's reported IDR1,752.6bn because the printed depreciation lines leave amortisation and other non-cash charges in the bridge [S0, S3, F89]. We keep it small and do not use it to set the target. The sales multiple is depressed because contractor revenue is a pass-through of client mine plans while the peer median embeds miners' commodity revenue [S0]. The DCF remains the anchor, and the weighted value of Rp179 sits inside the cross-check range.

The sensitivity table shows that terminal growth and margin for the contract business, and the GMR carrying value, dominate [S0]. A one-point change in WACC moves the DCF value by a large amount because the terminal value is discounted over the full horizon, which is why we treat the DCF as a value anchor rather than a precise price [S0]. The target is not set at the top of the range: the konglo lens is applied after the fundamental work and keeps the target close to the fundamental value, holding most of the small premium the shares carry today. The refreshed peer set is what moved the fundamental value this update — the peer EV/EBITDA median now reads 7.1x, lower than at the initiation, so the weighted value and the lens arithmetic have shifted; the operating assumptions are unchanged [S0].

What does today's price imply? The reverse DCF holds GMR at our probability-weighted bridge and solves for FY2027E revenue growth; at the current Rp262, the answer is 13.1% [S0]. That is above the house CPI forecast, implying positive real growth, and above the macro deck's nominal GDP anchor; the market is therefore pricing the contract business for faster-than-economy growth, not shrinkage. It is not marking GMR near zero — the bridge is worth more than half of the market capitalisation — but it is asking the contractor to compound above nominal GDP, a more optimistic view than our base case and the reason the shares now carry a premium to our fundamental value [S0, S4, S5, F19, F90].

The konglo lens is the second stage of the valuation and it is deliberately separate from the fundamental work. The engine measures the price at 1.45x our current fundamental value of Rp181 — Rp262 against that value — and keeps part of that premium for twelve months according to three regime scenarios; the same premium-kept arithmetic applied to our twelve-month value of Rp207 produces the base lens target [S0]. Because DEWA has no HSC listing, no enforcement action and a free float above the minimum [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026], the base regime closes 30% of the log premium, giving a base target of Rp268; the bear regime closes more of it at Rp231, and the bull regime lets it widen at Rp317 [S0]. The probability-weighted target is Rp271, above the twelve-month fundamental value because most of the small premium is kept, and we rate the stock HOLD [S0]. Two limits are worth stating. The lens is a deterministic function of the registry flags, not an analyst premium, and it can only move the target toward fundamental value; it cannot create value. And the GMR bridge is held at its weighted value in all three regimes, because the engine applies the valuation bridge to every scenario; the GMR-specific downside and upside are therefore described in the scenario section rather than shocked through the lens [S0, S5].

The dividend is not the anchor for this name. Twelve-month DPS is Rp3, a low yield, because the company has no fixed payout policy and prioritises capex, debt service and the buyback [S3, S4]. The FY2025 profit paid IDR58.6bn of cash dividend, and the model's FY2026E payout is 16.0% of earnings, so most cash is retained for the fleet and the balance sheet [S3, S4]. The market anchor is asset value — the GMR carrying value and the contract cash flows — not dividend capacity. We state that because the industry card expects a dividend-capacity cross-check; for DEWA the cross-check does not anchor the price, and the asset-value anchor is the right one.

The business scenarios are mirrored on the same two drivers, as the method requires. The base case holds our revenue and margin path. The bear case subtracts three points of revenue growth and one and a half points of gross margin every year, as the RKAB cut binds and the state-exporter transition disrupts KPC and Arutmin cargo scheduling; the bull case adds exactly the same amounts, as the owned fleet runs at full utilisation and service rates reset with inflation [S3, S7]. The probabilities are base 50%, bear 25% and bull 25%, and the resulting targets are Rp205, Rp167 and Rp250 [S0]. The base case is the most probable path, not the cautious one: the nine-month evidence supports the revenue run-rate and the recovered margin, and the bear requires the client volume decline to resume and the in-sourcing gain to be given back in rates.

GMR risk is now carried explicitly in the bridge rather than only described here. The base assumes only half of the IDR4,535.4bn KJPP appraisal uplift, because the asset has no resource, reserve or feasibility statement and is still not operating [S4, S5, F19, F90, F46, F109]; the other half is the probability weight the previous draft lacked. That half‑of‑the‑uplift weight flows into every scenario value, since the engine applies the valuation bridge to all three, so the probability-weighted target already embeds a half chance that the uplift is not real. The full-write-back tail is the IDR844.5bn consideration floor, which would remove the withheld half of the IDR4,535.4bn appraisal uplift and take the bear-case value below the current share price of Rp262; that is the honest downside and the reason the rating is fragile [S5, F18, F20, S0]. The mirror image is a resource statement that validates the appraisal, which would restore the withheld uplift as upside. A GMR write-back scenario therefore needs no separate fourth draw: it is the half‑withheld state already priced in the bridge, and we disclose the full-write-back arithmetic above [S0]. The business bear and bull remain mirrored on revenue growth and gross margin only.

The konglo regime scenarios are separate and independent of the business scenarios. The lens's bear regime closes more of the premium and targets Rp231; its base targets Rp268; its bull lets the premium widen and targets Rp317 [S0]. A business disappointment and a regime shift are different events: the first changes the fundamental value, the second changes how much of the gap between price and value the market closes. A reader should not add the two bear cases together. The dated regime catalysts are the free-float deadline on 31 March 2027, the MSCI consultation feedback by 30 April 2027 and its decision by 30 June 2027, and any HSC review or enforcement action; DEWA itself is compliant on float and not on the HSC list, so these act through the complex rather than the company [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026].

The downside risks, ranked by likelihood times impact: related-party contract risk (high impact, medium likelihood) because the clients supplied 97.7% of nine-month revenue and there is no arm's-length market to appeal to [S4, S5, F87]; refinancing and liquidity risk (high, medium), with bank loans of IDR2,268.9bn current and IDR2,306.0bn non-current against cash of IDR744.9bn, interest cover only a little over two times, and the newest facility at 10.0% [S4, F34, F59, F60, F61, F103, F104, F106]; regulatory risk (high, medium) from the RKAB cut to 600 million tonnes and the 1 January 2027 DSI window [S3, S7]; and GMR execution risk (high impact, unquantifiable likelihood) because there is no resource, reserve or feasibility statement [S5, F109]. Commodity and cost risk (medium, medium) comes from higher Brent and the B50 mandate, partly offset by pass-through [S3, S4]; operational risk (medium, medium) from weather, fleet availability and safety [S6]; capital-allocation risk (medium, already realised) from the buyback that authorised up to IDR950.0bn, paid IDR791.4bn of cash for 1,639 million shares above today's price, and left treasury stock at IDR951.7bn [S3, S4, F54, F67, F93, F107]. We found no disclosure that the treasury shares are pledged and withdraw the earlier statement that they are; if a pledge exists outside the reviewed filings, coverage at today's Rp262 would be weak [S3, S4, S0, F54, F67]. Governance and regime risk is high impact but low likelihood in the base: no HSC listing or enforcement today, though 2026 showed how fast the market can reprice concentrated-ownership names [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026].

The strongest case against us is simple: more than half of the fundamental equity value is an exploration asset valued by appraisal rather than a mine plan, inside a related-party contractor whose customers are its controlling group. If a reader marks GMR at its consideration, the fundamental value falls toward the current price and even the HOLD would be at risk. We accept that framing rather than argue it away, and keep the consideration floor in the base because the method card forbids an unsourced haircut below sourced sunk value; the appraisal uplift is in at half only [S5]. The HOLD is therefore GMR-weighted, not fleet-validated: 4.5% of total return is below the house ADD threshold, and the target clears the price only because the konglo lens retains part of the premium the shares already carry [S0].

The upside signposts are as important as the downside ones, and three are missing from the price. First, a renewed buyback at today's Rp262 would retire about a ninth of the capital (against the 1,639 million shares or about four percent retired in the 2026 buyback at an average well above today's price); the mechanism is direct per-share accretion and it is the cheapest use of the IDR951.7bn treasury capacity, but it is a capital-allocation event the revenue-and-margin scenario set does not capture [S7]. Second, the MSCI Indonesia Standalone consultation resolves by 30 June 2027, and DEWA at a 49.8% free float with no HSC listing or enforcement is the compliant vehicle in a group whose members fell by four-fifths or more; the mechanism is index-flow and re-rating of the float, a konglo-regime effect that sits in the lens's bull regime rather than the business scenarios [S8]. Third, spot Newcastle at US$150/t and HBA at US$127/t sit roughly a quarter to a third above the FY2027E markers of US$118/t and US$112/t, which supports client mine plans and therefore the IDR1,818.3bn related-party receivable; the mechanism is collection rather than new revenue, and it is a working-capital and impairment risk-reducer that the scenario set does not score [S0, S4, F68]. Conversely, the signposts that would change our view to the downside: a GMR resource statement failing to appear or a write-back; a KPC or Arutmin contract amendment on worse rates, or an early signal on renewal ahead of the Arutmin IUPK expiry on 1 November 2030 or the KPC IUPK expiry on 31 December 2031; a quarterly volume decline that breaks the in-sourcing margin; sustained capex above the 25.0% FY2026E rate without matching revenue; a refinancing at a higher rate or a fall in interest cover; and any HSC or enforcement action that changes the konglo regime flags [S0, S3, S4, S5, F91, F92]. GMR exploration success, a new non-related-party contract, or an acceleration of the konglo re-rating would move us toward the bull case.

DEWA is a Bakrie-group name in the house konglo registry (as-of 27 October 2026). The 31 December 2025 register lists Goldwave Capital at 9.4% (quoted for Zurich Assets), Zurich Assets International at 6.2%, PT Andhesti Tungkas Pratama at 8.5%, CIMB Securities at 6.4%, CGS International at 5.5%, public shareholders at 63.1% and treasury stock at 0.9% [S3, F96, F97, F98, F99, F100, F101, F102]; the FY2025 statements show the same lines at 9.4% to 5.5% [S5]. Goldwave and Zurich are linked in the register's own annotation and together are the largest identified bloc, so we withdraw the earlier statement that no holder sits above ten percent [S3, F96, F97]. Market data puts insider ownership at 44.7% and the free float at 49.8% [S0]. The registry records a free float of 49.8%, comfortably above the raised minimum, so DEWA is not caught by the free-float deadlines that pressure other konglo names; it records no HSC listing and no enforcement action against the company.

The conversion history explains why the register and the cap table differ. The February 2025 private placement issued 18,834 million shares in total — 10,093 million shares to PT Madhani Talatah Nusantara and smaller blocks to ATP and AMM — 46.3% of the post-issue capital at Rp75, and the filings call the recipients creditors, not related contractors [S3, S6, F55, F56, F94, F95]. The 31 December 2025 register shows no MTN or AMM line while ATP appears at 8.5%; the most likely reading is that MTN's block sits inside the public bucket or was sold, but the filings do not identify the transferee [S3, F98, F101]. We state the gap rather than assume an owner, and we withdraw the label "related contractors" for MTN, ATP and AMM because no reviewed source establishes a related-party link [S6].

The controller question is better answered by the related-party map than the register. KPC and Arutmin are entities under common control with DEWA and supply almost all revenue; the President Commissioner of DEWA is also President Commissioner of KPC and Arutmin and a director of Bumi Resources, so the board interlock is explicit [S3, S5]. That is the governance discount in one sentence: the customers, the controlling group and the board are the same ecosystem. Related-party revenue was 97.7% of the total in the first nine months of 2026 and 95.5% of FY2025 revenue, with KPC and Arutmin supplying IDR3,588.0bn and IDR1,395.0bn against third-party revenue of IDR119.0bn; related-party receivables were IDR1,818.3bn at the end of September 2026 [S3, S4, F27, F31, F32, F33, F68, F87]. The GMR acquisition was itself an affiliate transaction: 99.8% of GMR through the realisation of an advance of IDR844.5bn, with negative goodwill of IDR4,535.4bn booked to profit [S5, F18, F20, F46]. These are disclosed, but the related-party test is failed by construction; the only mitigant is that the transactions are audited and sit inside the same group economics.

On the structural flags, the 2025 debt-to-equity conversion issued new Series B shares at Rp75, converting debt into equity and cutting leverage [S3, S6]. The 2026 buyback authorised up to IDR950.0bn; the cash actually paid for treasury shares in the first nine months of 2026 was IDR791.4bn, and IDR951.7bn of treasury stock was still carried at 30 September 2026, so the shares are held in treasury rather than retired and the share count is issued less treasury [S3, S4, F67, F93, F107]. That was a transfer from continuing shareholders to selling holders at an average well above today's Rp262, and it used cash the balance sheet needed for the refinancing; we treat it as a capital-allocation failure. We could not find disclosure that the treasury shares are pledged and withdraw the earlier statement that they are; if a pledge exists, coverage at today's price would be weak [S3, S4, S0, F54, F67]. The asset-security package over more than half of net assets was approved at a shareholders' meeting in 2025 [S6]. These are structure flags, not manipulation flags.

Audit and disclosure are adequate: the FY2025 statements were audited by PKF Hadiwinata, which replaced RSM AAJ, with an unmodified opinion and no non-audit services [S3]; the auditor change is worth monitoring. The dividend record is thin and discretionary — no fixed payout policy, and the FY2025 profit paid IDR58.6bn, a small fraction of reported and underlying profit [S3, S4]. ESG exposures are those of a coal-services contractor: the energy transition through its client base, rehabilitation and mine-closure obligations, and the social licence of operations in Kalimantan and Aceh. It holds ISO certifications and reports zero-accident awards at the Bengalon and Asam Asam projects [S6]; GMR adds an Aceh exploration and permitting dimension not yet developed enough to assess [S5]. We do not apply an ESG discount to the valuation.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The nearest hard data point is the full-year 2026 result in the first quarter of 2027, which will show whether the nine-month margin held through the fourth quarter [S4]. The 1 January 2027 state-exporter transition is the next regulatory event, and the market will watch the first cargoes through PT DSI closely [S7]. The free-float deadline and the MSCI decision are regime events for the konglo complex rather than company-specific ones, but they set the backdrop for how fast the gap to our twelve-month value can close [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026]. The contract catalysts are dated and long: the Arutmin IUPK to 1 November 2030 and the KPC IUPK to 31 December 2031, when the terminal value becomes a renewal question [S5, F91, F92].

The KPIs we monitor are: overburden removal and coal production volumes and the in-house versus subcontractor split; gross margin and the subcontractor, repair and fuel lines; related-party receivables and collection days; gross debt, cash, the refinancing calendar and interest cover; capex against the 25.0% FY2026E run-rate; the treasury-share carrying value; and any GMR exploration disclosure [S0, S3, S4, S5]. We also watch HSC status, free-float compliance, index deletions and enforcement actions [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026]. A change in any of these would trigger an update or a revision rather than a silent drift.

For Indonesian contractors, the most reliable early warning of a margin problem is not the reported gross margin but the subcontractor share of material moved: when a contractor leans back on subcontractors, the variable cost rises before the margin line shows it. The second is receivables from affiliated clients, which can lengthen without a credit event because the group allocates cash centrally. Both are worth tracking quarterly.

bear.narrative: The client-volume decline of 2024-25 continues (KPC overburden 122.09 to 102.16 million bcm and coal 9.69 to 10.51 Mt; Arutmin coal 7.46 to 6.53 Mt [F71, F73, F74, F76, F80, F82, S3]), the RKAB cut to about 600 Mt binds harder and the 1 January 2027 PT DSI export handover disrupts KPC and Arutmin cargo scheduling, so revenue growth runs three points below base and gross margin 1.5 points lower as the subcontractor mix is rebuilt. The GMR bridge is applied to every engine scenario; in this state of the world the appraisal is not validated and the asset is written back toward its Rp844.5bn consideration [F20, S5], which is a further downside not captured in the mechanical bear value.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same drivers: client volumes stabilise as KPC and Arutmin keep their allocations through the RKAB cut, the Arutmin extension wins new Kintap scope, revenue growth runs three points above base and service rates reset with fuel and wage inflation so gross margin holds 1.5 points higher. A GMR resource statement that validates the Rp5,380bn bridge would be a further upside of the same order as the bear's write-down and is not included in the mechanical bull value.

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 revenue was Rp5,102.0bn, +9.7% yoy [F28, F70, S4], but the LK does not publish quarterly physical volumes and the growth is not volume-led: KPC revenue rose to Rp3,588.0bn from Rp3,088.0bn while KPC's own FY2025 mine output fell (overburden 102.16 from 106.33 million bcm, coal 10.51 from 11.21 Mt), and Arutmin revenue was Rp1,395.0bn against Rp1,357.9bn on flat tonnage [F31, F32, F71, F72, F74, F75, F84, F85, S3, S4]. Third-party revenue fell to Rp119.0bn from Rp204.4bn [F33, F86, S4]. The 9M growth is therefore rate, mix and the Arutmin extension, not a volume cycle. FY2026E +8.5% carries the 9M run-rate into a seasonally stronger Q4 but below the nine-month pace; FY2027E +5% is a real-rate step-up on flat-to-down client volumes, and FY2028E-FY2030E decelerate to +4%, +3.5% and +3% as the 2026 coal RKAB of about 600 Mt from about 790 Mt [F38, F39, S3] and the 1 January 2027 state-exporter transition through PT DSI [S7] cap client offtake. No FY2027E-FY2030E mine-plan volume schedule is public; we do not invent one and instead hold volumes flat with rate inflation. LT 3.0% is IDR CPI plus modest real growth, below the macro deck's nominal GDP anchor.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The in-sourcing turnaround is the single biggest margin driver: FY2025 gross margin was 15.05% on revenue of Rp6,392.8bn and COGS of Rp5,430.6bn [F1, F3, S5], while 9M-2026 gross margin reached 20.28% (revenue Rp5,102.0bn, COGS Rp4,067.2bn) [F28, F58, S4] as subcontractor cost fell to Rp593.4bn from Rp1,137.8bn in the nine-month 2025 comparative and the owned fleet took over more waste removal [F62, S4, S6]. The input is stated AT FY2025 BASE FUEL COSTS, as the template requires. An input of 22.6% reproduces the realised 9M-2026 effective margin of 20.28% once the deck's FY2026 Brent (96.0) is put through the 15%/50% oil link; the previous 22.2% input was about half a point too low. We then hold the input flat in nominal terms for FY2027E-FY2030E and the long run: costs stay at the last actual in real terms, as the method card requires. The effective margin therefore moves only with the oil link (higher in FY2027E at the lower Brent deck), not through a default wage or biodiesel squeeze. There is no sourced cost line that justifies a multi-point decline.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel is a direct COGS line of Rp210.75bn in 9M-2026 (5.2% of Rp4,067.2bn COGS) [S4] and diesel also sits inside equipment rental (Rp378.0bn) and hauling (Rp427.1bn) [S4]. Adding the contractor-supplied fuel embedded in those two lines gives about 15% of COGS exposed to Brent; the rest (depreciation, wages, repairs, subcontractors) is not oil-linked.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Operating agreements with KPC and Arutmin are rate-based and renewed periodically; the company absorbed the 2025 B40 cost increase without a full rate reset [S3], so only half of the oil exposure is assumed to pass through into service rates in the same year, the balance sits in the margin until the next contract reset.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 SG&A was 3.69% of revenue (Rp235.8bn of Rp6,392.8bn) [S5]; 9M-2026 was 6.32% (Rp322.4bn of Rp5,102.0bn) [S4], including a jump in salaries and wages (Rp208.8bn vs Rp116.5bn) and a new depreciation charge in G&A after the fleet purchase. Note 27 of the interim LK explains neither the salary step nor any one-off item, so we do not assume it reverses: the input is held at the observed nine-month run-rate. That removes the earlier unsourced normalisation, which was the largest value-positive departure in the base.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: D&A is the data pack's biggest error: Yahoo carries Rp19.1bn for FY2025 because the LK uses the direct cash-flow method. The LK prints the components separately, fixed-asset depreciation of Rp861.96bn (S5 p.89) plus right-of-use depreciation of Rp78.71bn (S5 p.92), and F9 carries their combined FY2025 total of Rp940.67bn, which is the figure the model uses; F9 is therefore cited for the combined total, not for the fixed-asset component alone, and adding F10 on top of it would double-count. The company's own EBITDA bridge of Rp1,752.6bn less operating profit of Rp726.4bn [F88, F89, S3] implies about Rp1,026bn of total non-cash charge, i.e. a further ~Rp85bn of amortisation/other non-cash that the LK does not print as a single line. 9M-2026 printed totals were Rp826.2bn of fixed-asset depreciation plus Rp19.1bn of right-of-use depreciation, 16.6% of 9M revenue [F110, F111, S4]. FY2026E 15.5% of revenue (higher Q4 revenue dilutes the ratio), easing to 15.0% LT as the fleet depreciates on a straight-line basis; the model's FY2025 da line uses the F9 combined total, with the residual to the company bridge disclosed in §3 rather than forced into D&A.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex peaked with the two fleet batches: Rp1,588.9bn in FY2025 (24.9% of revenue) and Rp1,436.0bn in FY2024 [F11, F12, S5], and 9M-2026 was Rp1,341.6bn [F52, S4], flat with the 9M-2025 Rp1,338.2bn and equal to 26.3% of 9M revenue, not a step-down. The Oct-2026 Rp149.2bn Bank Mega investment credit to subsidiary PT DH Kontraktama, explicitly for heavy-equipment purchase, confirms the programme continued after the balance-sheet date [F105, S10]. FY2026E is therefore set at 25% of revenue, close to the 9M run-rate; FY2027E 21%, then 19%, 18%, 17% and 16% LT as the two batches are complete (fully operational by end-September 2025 [S6]) and spend settles toward a maintenance level for the completed fleet. The October credit is a further heavy-equipment purchase, so the fleet is still growing at the margin, not only being replaced [F105, S10]. LT 16% is above D&A at 15% of revenue [F9], so the fleet is maintained rather than run down.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The 9M-2026 balance sheet shows operating working capital of Rp21.8bn, effectively zero against Rp5,102.0bn of revenue [S4]; FY2025 was negative (Rp-227.6bn) because related-party receivables and payables net close. A contractor paid by two related-party mine operators has no structural working-capital build, so 0% is the anchor.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Indonesia's corporate rate is 22%; 9M-2026 tax expense of Rp146.8bn on PBT of Rp659.9bn is a 22.2% effective rate [S4]. FY2025's apparent tax benefit is the deferred-tax effect of the negative goodwill, not a sustainable rate [S5].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The 9M-2026 finance cost of Rp319.4bn [F61, S4] is a nine-month charge, not an annual rate: annualised on opening debt of Rp3,559.4bn it is about 12.0%, and on average debt of about Rp4,095bn about 10.4%. The new Bank Mega equipment credit signed on 29 October 2026 carries 10% per annum [F106, S10], and the July-2025 syndicated facility was 8.3% but was repaid on 22 January 2026 [S3]. 10.0% is the blended marginal rate used for the P&L interest charge in the forecast only; it does not replace the cost of debt in the WACC, which continues to use the house 9.45% pre-tax rate (val.coc.kd_pre_tax), so the house floor still sets the discount rate.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 finance income of Rp5.57bn on opening cash of Rp1,590.6bn is a 0.35% nine-month yield [S4]; the operating cash balance is largely transactional, so 1.0% is already generous against the realised run-rate and well below the BI rate of 5.75% in the macro deck.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The 9M-2026 cash flow statement shows gross bank loans drawn of Rp5,041.7bn and repaid of Rp3,984.6bn, a net increase in gross bank debt of Rp1,057.1bn [S4 p.13]. Lease liabilities fell by Rp36.2bn and other long-term payables by Rp523.3bn net, so total debt rose by about Rp1,070.9bn to Rp4,630.3bn at 30 September 2026 [F103, F104, S4]. The forecast uses that actual gross-debt change, not the change in net debt: the Rp1,917bn net-debt increase in the prior draft double-counted the Rp845.7bn cash decline. The model's single borrowing line cannot also carry the Rp791.4bn treasury purchase or the Rp624.6bn other-payables repayment, which are financing outflows that do not change gross bank debt [F34, F107, S4 p.13]. The year-end cash bridge, all from the LK or from our own forecast: opening cash Rp1,590.6bn + nine-month operating cash Rp1,664.8bn [F108] + Q4 operating forecast Rp406.5bn (FY np Rp689.8bn + D&A Rp1,075.1bn less 9M np Rp513.1bn and 9M D&A Rp845.3bn) - nine-month investing Rp2,158.2bn [F112] - Q4 capex Rp392.4bn (FY capex Rp1,734.0bn less 9M Rp1,341.6bn) - nine-month financing Rp352.4bn [F113] = Rp758.9bn year-end cash, close to the Rp744.9bn at 30 September because Q4 is roughly cash-neutral. The model's FY2026E cash line of Rp2,403.8bn is Rp1,644.9bn higher, and the difference is fully allocated: the model's operating cash of Rp1,537.3bn is Rp534.0bn below the LK's Rp2,071.3bn; the model's investing of Rp1,734.0bn is Rp816.6bn below the LK's Rp2,550.6bn (advances for fixed assets Rp444.9bn, exploration Rp31.9bn, other non-current placements Rp51.5bn, other current assets Rp288.2bn); and the model's financing of Rp1,009.9bn is Rp1,362.3bn above the LK's -Rp352.4bn (treasury Rp791.4bn, net other-long-term-payables repayment Rp523.3bn, lease payments Rp36.2bn, share-issuance costs Rp3.7bn, other Rp7.7bn).
